title: Pascal's Triangle Revisited

jokes.text: Jeff tells Professor Whitman he hopes he'll be 'seizing a more contemporary movie'
jokes.setup: Professor Whitman (a 'carpe diem' type, referencing Dead Poets Society) tells Jeff he hopes he'll be 'seizing the day this summer'
jokes.punchline: Jeff fires back wishing Whitman would seize a more contemporary movie — puncturing the professor's whole shtick by calling out the dated source material
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff wit — it's sharp, economic, and perfectly character-integrated. Only Jeff would dismiss a professor's sincere life advice with a snide pop-culture dig. The structure is tight: the setup gives us the cliché, Jeff immediately deflates it. Scores high because it does real comedic work in very few words while revealing character.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Whitman
dialogue.line: Seize the day.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, maybe update your movie references. That came out in 1989.

jokes.text: Jeff compliments Leonard ('Looking good, Leonard'), then asks 'Stroke or tai chi?'
jokes.setup: Jeff is in a breezy, end-of-year good mood, casually complimenting people
jokes.punchline: He can't tell if the elderly Leonard is doing tai chi or having a medical emergency — delivered as casual small talk
jokes.explanation: Dark and efficient — the joke weaponizes Leonard's age and frailty with cheerful nonchalance. The deadpan delivery of a genuinely dark question as casual pleasantry is the whole joke, and it lands. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Is that exercise or a medical emergency?

jokes.text: Jeff tells Garrett 'Keep up whatever it is you're doing' and Garrett says 'It's called chillaxing. Duh!'
jokes.setup: Jeff is making his rounds with cheerful, vague compliments to background characters
jokes.punchline: Garrett interprets the deliberately vague compliment as ignorance of a specific activity he's doing, and defensively names it 'chillaxing' — the joke is on the word itself and Garrett's earnest delivery
jokes.explanation: Functional background-character comedy. 'Chillaxing. Duh!' is funny because of Garrett's specific energy, but the joke itself is fairly thin. It works more as a texture moment than a crafted bit.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: Chillaxing. It's a state of being where you achieve maximum relaxation through the systematic elimination of stress and tension. It's not just about lying around — it's a philosophy.

jokes.text: Britta's ex-boyfriend (Vaughn) lingers awkwardly while Jeff is trying to leave, and Jeff gives him a litany of uncomfortable greetings: 'Hello, good morning, howdy'
jokes.setup: Vaughn approaches Jeff and seems to want to talk; Jeff is clearly hoping to exit the interaction
jokes.punchline: Jeff cycles through multiple casual greetings in rapid succession — a social coping mechanism that reveals he has no idea how to handle the encounter
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Jeff's social anxiety manifesting as over-casual deflection. The triple greeting is a recognizable human behavior exaggerated to comic effect. Not exceptional but well-observed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Not much could ruin today.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, did I just jinx myself? That's a sitcom trope. I literally just tempted fate.

jokes.text: Jeff says 'I got class in, like, five hours' as an excuse to ditch Vaughn
jokes.setup: Jeff needs an excuse to get away from Vaughn
jokes.punchline: He uses 'class in five hours' as an urgent reason to leave — the joke is the absurdity of treating five hours as imminent, while also satirizing Jeff's laziness and poor excuses
jokes.explanation: Economical character joke — it only works because we know Jeff is both socially slippery and academically lazy. The 'five hours' detail is specific enough to be funny.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Okay, your turn. Give me a celebrity and I'll combine it with banana.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Denzel Washington.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Denzel Banana-ington.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's just adding banana to the end.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. Banana Denzel Washington.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The Pope.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Banana Pope.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: A fire truck.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Banana fire truck.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're not even trying anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You're right. Okay. Banana banana banana.

jokes.text: Britta: 'I finally get to click send on so many I told you so emails'
jokes.setup: Britta is celebrating finishing her first year of college
jokes.punchline: Instead of a sentimental reflection, she reveals her first instinct is petty vindication — she's been composing 'I told you so' emails all year
jokes.explanation: Very strong character joke. Britta's self-righteous, slightly insufferable personality is perfectly crystallized — she's not celebrating growth, she's celebrating being right. The specificity of 'click send' makes it modern and vivid. High character integration because it really could only be Britta.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm ready to play the banana game.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Alright, just eat the banana.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna make love to this banana.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What? Why are you looking at me like that? It's just a banana!

jokes.text: Britta: 'Oh, shoot. I forgot saying that summons him.'
jokes.setup: The Dean has appeared immediately after Jeff said nothing could ruin today
jokes.punchline: Britta acknowledges the sitcom logic — that complaining about him summons him — treating it as an in-universe rule they've all discovered
jokes.explanation: Very good meta-awareness joke. Community's signature move — characters treating sitcom logic as literal reality. 'Summons him' treats the Dean like a supernatural entity, which is both funny in itself and a smart commentary on recurring-character tropes. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I remember laughing at 'teacher's aids' in elementary school.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's funny.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Then in seventh grade, we found out Mr. Henderson actually had AIDS.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's dark.

jokes.text: The Dean announces: 'Some folks say transfer formal isn't really rolling off the tongue, so we're just gonna call it The Tranny Dance!'
jokes.setup: The Dean is trying to rebrand the transfer formal to something catchier
jokes.punchline: 'The Tranny Dance' — the Dean presents an obviously inappropriate abbreviation with complete sincerity and institutional authority
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean obliviousness joke — he's not malicious, just monumentally unaware. The humor comes from institutional cluelessness presented with bureaucratic pride. The callback to 'Tranny Queen' sashes later deepens the joke. Character-specific: only Greendale's Dean could do this with such earnest sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I take the boys on trips all the time. I just tell them those places with the hourly rates are 'adventure hotels.'

jokes.text: Pierce says 'banana penis' trying to decode the word game, then says 'Sure, you would've loved it if he did it' to Troy
jokes.setup: The group is playing a word-substitution game (replacing a word with 'banana'); Pierce tries to participate
jokes.punchline: Pierce lands on 'banana penis' and when the others react, he accuses Troy of only objecting because Pierce said it — revealing Pierce's paranoid defensiveness about being out of the loop
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke — the punchline 'banana penis' is lowbrow but Pierce saying it is funnier than a younger character saying it. The follow-up accusation at Troy is actually the better beat, revealing Pierce's insecurity about group belonging.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Gary's transferring? Oh no, that's terrible!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Wait, really? Oh thank God.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Gary's leaving? Best news I've heard all week.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Pierce! Shirley! We should be sad for him.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Honey, Gary ate my potato salad without asking.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Gary told me my jokes were offensive. Which they are, but coming from him?

jokes.text: Pierce: 'What's happened to you and me, Troy? Remember how hard we laughed when we first heard the term teacher's aids?' / Troy: 'Yeah.' / Pierce: 'And then we found out a teacher did have AIDS.'
jokes.setup: Pierce tries to bond with Troy by reminiscing about shared laughter over a misheard phrase
jokes.punchline: The innocent malapropism ('teacher's aids' vs. 'teacher has AIDS') reveals the dark reality — and Pierce recounts it with complete nostalgia, as if it's a fond memory
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is nearly perfect: Pierce sets up a sweet nostalgia-bonding beat, Troy plays along, then the dark pivot hits. The joke works on multiple levels — it's a wordplay/mishearing joke, a dark joke about AIDS, AND a character joke about Pierce's obliviousness to what's appropriate. The pacing (the beat between Troy's 'Yeah' and Pierce's reveal) is masterful. It's genuinely quotable and subversive. Earns 8+ because it's exceptional on structure, character integration, and economy — all in service of a genuinely surprising dark punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: There's a transfer queen contest every year. It's like a pageant, but for people who've switched schools.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The winner gets a sash, a crown, and they're featured in the community college newsletter.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I was the transfer queen last year. It was the best day of my life.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: And if anyone else wins this year, I will kill them.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Money's tight, so I hope I can convince them for one more year that motels are tiny, little theme parks.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is discussing summer plans with the group — taking the boys on a trip
jokes.punchline: He plans to deceive children into thinking motels are fun destinations — the joke is in the specific, detailed lie and his matter-of-fact delivery
jokes.explanation: Surprisingly warm-but-dark Pierce joke. The image of a sad motel reframed as a 'tiny little theme park' is vivid and specific. It works because it's simultaneously depressing and kind-of-sweet — Pierce is trying, in his oblivious way. Good character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Why do you keep showing up whenever something goes wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm the Dean. It's my job to be here when there's a problem.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, I mean... you literally appear. Like I summoned you or something.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: That's ridiculous. I have a very busy schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Then why are you here right now?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Because things went wrong.

jokes.text: Troy: 'My dad wants me to leave the nest, so he feels less weird that his girlfriend is 20.'
jokes.setup: Troy explains he needs to find somewhere to live
jokes.punchline: His dad isn't kicking him out for healthy reasons — it's to reduce the awkwardness of dating someone Troy's age
jokes.explanation: Very economical dark joke. The line does a lot of work in one sentence — reveals family dysfunction, makes a clichéd situation (dad dating a young woman) specific and strange, and subverts the 'leaving the nest' metaphor hilariously. High economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: The name is a bit awkward, isn't it? 'Greendale Community College Dance.' That spells...

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We could call it the 'Pelton's Annual Gala Celebration.' That spells P.A.G.C.

jokes.text: Abed: 'You could live in a pyramid.' (non-sequitur response to Troy's housing problem)
jokes.setup: Troy says he needs to find a place to live; the group starts thinking
jokes.punchline: Abed suggests a pyramid with no context or explanation — pure lateral, unhelpful Abed logic
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed non-sequitur — the joke IS the total non-sequitur logic delivered deadpan. High character integration (only Abed would say this), but the joke is thin. Gets a chuckle from audience familiarity with Abed's pattern.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I just feel like nobody understands me.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: You're doing it again. You're lying on a couch, talking about your feelings, speaking in movie therapy clichés.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's what therapy is!

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: No, it's not. Real therapy is awkward and uncomfortable, not a Woody Allen film.

jokes.text: The group's reaction to Gary transferring: 'Oh good.' / 'Finally.' / 'Thank God.' / 'Hope he transfers to hell.'
jokes.setup: Annie mentions her friend Gary is transferring and will be at the dance
jokes.punchline: The whole group immediately reveals they hate Gary through escalating dismissals, culminating in Pierce's 'Hope he transfers to hell'
jokes.explanation: Good ensemble joke with escalation structure. Gary is a named character we've never seen and the group hates him unanimously — the joke is on the ensemble's collective pettiness. 'Hope he transfers to hell' is the best beat. The escalation from 'finally' to 'thank god' to 'hell' is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: This is our last session.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You dumbass.

jokes.text: Annie explains what transfer queen is — 'It's like prom queen. You wear a sash.' — and then completely breaks: 'and I am SO jealous, Britta, I want to murder you.'
jokes.setup: Annie is calmly explaining the transfer queen nomination to Britta
jokes.punchline: The explanation suddenly pivots into a confession of murderous jealousy — total tonal whiplash delivered with Annie's specific barely-contained-feelings energy
jokes.explanation: Excellent Annie character joke. The structure — a calm, helpful explanation that suddenly ruptures into intense jealous rage — perfectly captures Annie's type-A suppression. 'I want to murder you' is the kind of surprising line that only works because of how straight Annie delivers it. High character integration: this is quintessential Annie Edison. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Mental illness is like a dinosaur suit—it looks impressive from the outside, but inside you're just a homeless guy sweating through a felt costume, wondering how you got here.

jokes.text: Dean: announces the nominees will be identified with sashes that say 'Tranny Queen' — and says 'Much more Greendale'
jokes.setup: The Dean is continuing to explain the dance logistics
jokes.punchline: 'Tranny Queen' on the sashes — callback to 'The Tranny Dance' naming — plus his proud editorial 'Much more Greendale' as if inappropriate naming is a Greendale brand value
jokes.explanation: 'Much more Greendale' is the real joke here — the Dean treats institutional inappropriateness as a feature, not a bug. Good callback payoff, and the institutional pride angle is strong character work.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: This nomination could really help you.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Queen of the dingbats.

jokes.text: Britta lying on the therapist's couch: 'You know, you don't actually have to lie on a sofa like it's a Woody Allen movie.' / Britta: 'Thank you for telling me that in the last session, dumbass.'
jokes.setup: Britta is in therapy; the therapist belatedly informs her she doesn't have to lie on the couch
jokes.punchline: Britta calls him a dumbass for not telling her sooner — she's been suffering through bad couch posture for sessions because of an unspoken assumption
jokes.explanation: Smart joke about therapy clichés — the Woody Allen reference is a sharp cultural shorthand, and Britta's frustrated 'dumbass' response is perfectly her. The joke subverts the therapy scene expectation while staying in character.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: The therapy is free.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, that explains a lot.

jokes.text: Therapist describes Britta's psychological issues: 'bugs on the windshield of your mind you may never be able to squeegee, like a certain birthday party attended by a rather enterprising transient in a dinosaur costume'
jokes.setup: The therapist is explaining Britta's psychological baggage using a metaphor
jokes.punchline: The metaphor becomes increasingly strange and specific — culminating in 'an enterprising transient in a dinosaur costume' as a casually referenced traumatic event
jokes.explanation: Genuinely original and vivid. The escalating specificity — windshield metaphor becoming a birthday party becoming a transient in a dinosaur costume — is a great absurdist escalation. We get the impression of a fully-developed dark backstory with no explanation, which is funnier than any explanation could be. High originality because that specific image is memorable and strange.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: You might want to be careful with that lipstick. It looks like a coin purse.

jokes.text: Britta: 'So you think I'd feel better about myself if I got all sexed up, went over there, and really tried to be crowned queen of the dingbats?'
jokes.setup: The therapist has suggested that winning the transfer queen crown might help Britta's self-esteem
jokes.punchline: Britta reframes the therapist's earnest advice through her anti-establishment filter — 'queen of the dingbats' perfectly encapsulates her contempt for the whole exercise
jokes.explanation: Strong Britta voice. 'Queen of the dingbats' is the right phrase for her worldview — contemptuous but slightly archaic, which is very Britta. The joke is in the gap between the therapist's clinical framing and Britta's translation of it.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Jeff, we're friends, right? I need your help with something.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, we're not friends, Chang. But I have a proposal for you.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: How about instead of pretending to be friends, we just agree to be cruel to each other on a regular basis?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's more honest, and frankly, it'll save us both a lot of time.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Wow, guess you really get what you pay for with free therapy.' / Therapist: 'Ouch. That stung a little bit.'
jokes.setup: The therapist has given advice Britta finds shallow
jokes.punchline: Britta nails him with a devastating one-liner about free therapy; the therapist's admission that it stung is the second laugh — he's not even professionally above it
jokes.explanation: Economically perfect two-beat joke. The line 'you get what you pay for with free therapy' is sharp and quotable, and the therapist's wounded 'that stung a little bit' transforms the moment — suddenly the professional veneer drops. Good two-character interaction that rewards both performers.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Ha!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: That laugh was too much.

jokes.text: Jeff's pre-emptive advice to Britta before she can tell him what the therapist said: 'He listens to you talk for a year, then recommends a makeover.'
jokes.setup: Britta and Jeff encounter each other, and Britta is about to relay what therapy suggested
jokes.punchline: Jeff cuts her off with a correctly-guessed summary — the therapist's 'profound' advice was just 'get a makeover'
jokes.explanation: Good economy — Jeff's ability to boil therapy down to 'listen for a year, recommend a makeover' is both cynical and accurate. Doubles as a jab at Britta for needing the advice confirmed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We can talk about this maturely.

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: You're right. I invented a medication for people who state the obvious.

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: It's called Jeffanol.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Well, don't wear as much lipstick as you did on Valentine's Day. Your mouth looked like a coin purse.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is offering unsolicited styling advice for the makeover/dance
jokes.punchline: 'Your mouth looked like a coin purse' — a weirdly specific, slightly cruel image that is funny precisely because of its oddness
jokes.explanation: 'Coin purse' is a great insult — oddly specific and strangely vivid. It's not the most elegant construction but the image sticks, which is why it scores high on quotability. Very Jeff: casually cruel but precise.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Your mom's so fat, when she sits around the study table, she REALLY sits around the study table.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That is a good idea. We should rearrange the furniture.

jokes.text: Chang to Jeff: 'Cheat my way through school.' [after Jeff was about to ask something else entirely]
jokes.setup: Chang approaches Jeff saying he needs help 'as a teacher and as my friend'
jokes.punchline: Before Jeff can even speculate, Chang pre-empts with 'Cheat my way through school' — both completing the sentence and making the ask explicit, skipping all pretense
jokes.explanation: Chang's total lack of filter is well-deployed here — the joke is in the absence of any social pretense. The setup of 'as a teacher and as my friend' makes the bluntness of the ask funnier. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I just realized I spend all my time at your place. I'm basically living there.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What? No, you're not.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I have a drawer at your apartment, Troy. A drawer. That's couple stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's just a drawer!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We eat breakfast together every morning. We have inside jokes. We finish each other's sentences.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Okay, those are just friend things.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Troy, I think we need to talk about what this is.

jokes.text: Jeff's counterproposal to Chang's request for help cheating: 'How about I point out to you that we've never actually been friends, then laugh at your very well-deserved misfortune? Let's just try that a second.'
jokes.setup: Chang approaches Jeff as a 'friend' and asks him to help him cheat through school
jokes.punchline: Jeff reframes his refusal as a formal 'counterproposal' — adding the meta-structure of a business negotiation to pure mockery
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The formal 'counterproposal' framing is pitch-perfect Jeff Winger — he can't just say no, he has to structure the humiliation like a legal brief. 'Very well-deserved misfortune' has just the right level of precise cruelty, and 'let's just try that a second' makes the cruelty active and ongoing rather than a one-off. High on structure, character integration, and earned quality. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh, it's not you. Abed hates America.

jokes.text: Jeff laughs at Chang and Chang responds: 'No, Jorge, you killed it.' (apparently to someone nearby)
jokes.setup: Jeff has laughed at Chang after his counterproposal
jokes.punchline: Chang talks to a nearby stranger ('Jorge') as if Jeff's laugh wasn't the one that counts — a face-saving deflection that's sadder than saying nothing
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat — Chang's pathetic pivot to complimenting a bystander is a funny way to save face. The specificity of 'Jorge' adds texture. It's secondary to the Jeff joke but adds a nice coda.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Dude, did you know hacky sack was invented by a Swedish guy named Soren Kierkegaardsson? He was like, the greatest hacky sack player of all time. They say he could keep a hacky sack in the air for like three days straight.

jokes.text: Jeff to Professor Slater (his ex): 'Before I respond to that, I'll have to take an extra-strength vitamin duh.'
jokes.setup: Slater, Jeff's ex, acknowledges she may have handled their breakup poorly and implies she made a mistake
jokes.punchline: Jeff's comeback: 'vitamin duh' — framing the obvious acknowledgment as something requiring a pharmaceutical dose of 'duh'
jokes.explanation: 'Vitamin duh' is a compact, memorable phrase. The joke transforms a sarcastic reaction into a quasi-medical metaphor — 'I need to prepare for this obvious statement'. It's very Jeff and quotable. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm worried we won't see each other as much.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Annie, we have texting, email, FaceTime. Separation isn't dramatic anymore. It's just inconvenient.

jokes.text: Abed to Jeff at the kegger: 'Funny... I spend so much time here, I forget that we don't live together. Then I think... what if we lived together?'
jokes.setup: Abed and Jeff are hanging out at Abed's kegger; Abed says this in a confessional, intimate way
jokes.punchline: Abed's social literalness turns a normal 'I like hanging out with you' thought into an unsettling domestic proposal, delivered with his characteristic flat sincerity
jokes.explanation: Very strong Abed character moment. The joke comes from his inability to understand social norms around expressing attachment — what most people would leave as an internal feeling, Abed says out loud with total directness. The pause ('Then I think...') and Jeff's silence create perfect cringe discomfort. Near-perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I was just... going to touch your hair.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No reason. I don't know.

jokes.text: Troy is told his girlfriend's boyfriend just got offered a spot on 'the number-one community-college hacky sack team in the nation'
jokes.setup: Vaughn announces his big news with the energy of someone who's been drafted to the NFL
jokes.punchline: It's the number-one community-college hacky sack team — the grandiosity of the announcement versus the niche/minor nature of the achievement is the joke
jokes.explanation: 'Number-one community-college hacky sack team' is a good joke target — it's specific enough to be funny and the pride is totally sincere. The gap between Vaughn's enthusiasm and the reality is the classic joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're so guarded. Like, emotionally guarded.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: See? You flinched.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I didn't even do anything. I just moved my hand near your face.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So come on, tell me I'm right.

jokes.text: Vaughn: 'I could be the next Yngwe Mackadangdang junior.'
jokes.setup: Vaughn is explaining the magnitude of the hacky sack opportunity
jokes.punchline: He invokes the name of a presumed hacky sack legend — 'Yngwe Mackadangdang junior' — as if this is a household name everyone should know
jokes.explanation: 'Yngwe Mackadangdang junior' is a genuinely great absurdist name — it feels simultaneously like a parody of a Scandinavian name and a made-up street name, and the 'junior' implies a dynasty. The name does most of the work. High originality and quotability because nobody could have predicted that specific word construction.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I feel amazing! This stuff is incredible!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait... why is the room spinning? Oh no, I can't feel my legs!

jokes.text: Jeff reaches to move Britta's hair as a romantic gesture, then completely backtracks: 'Well, you had hair I was gonna move.' / 'I don't know.'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta are having a tense/charged moment; Jeff reaches for her hair in what appears to be a romantic gesture
jokes.punchline: He loses his nerve mid-gesture and explains it in the most awkward possible way: 'You had hair I was gonna move' — passive construction, no accountability, total embarrassment
jokes.explanation: 'You had hair I was gonna move' is one of the episode's best lines — possibly the most quotable. It perfectly captures Jeff's pathological inability to be vulnerable: he converts a romantic gesture into bureaucratic passive voice. 'You had hair I was gonna move' reads like a witness statement to avoid liability. The structure is perfect (romantic setup → humiliating backtrack) and it is deeply character-specific. Earns 8+: comparable to the 8.0 anchor in wit and economy, and exceeds it in character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line:
♪ Greendale, Greendale, where the students come to learn,
We twist and shout in our underwear, as we take our turn,
Welding torches burning bright, and our panties in the air,
Greendale, Greendale, that's our Alma Mater fair! ♪

jokes.text: Britta asks 'Have you ever thought of yourself as a guarded person?' — proves it by suddenly reaching toward Jeff's face — he visibly flinches violently
jokes.setup: Britta suggests Jeff is guarded; she decides to demonstrate rather than argue
jokes.punchline: She reaches toward him (mirror of his own hair gesture) and his reflexive flinch proves her point immediately — the physical gag embodies the character argument
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant. Britta says 'watch' and proves Jeff's guardedness through action, turning his defensive flinch into the punchline. This is a callback (mirror of the hair gesture), it's physical comedy, and it makes a character argument simultaneously. Near-perfect economy — the whole thing takes about five words and a gesture. Earns 8+ for how much work it does in how little space.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: That was a venerable piece, Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: By which I mean old.

jokes.text: Professor Slater showing up at the kegger: 'Oh, you know, end of the year, randomly wandering.'
jokes.setup: Britta is surprised to see Professor Slater at the student party
jokes.punchline: 'Randomly wandering' — Slater's transparently false explanation for why she's at a student party where her ex-boyfriend happens to be
jokes.explanation: Functional — the flimsy excuse is funny in context, especially as we know why she's really there. Understated delivery makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm leaving with Vaughn.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's the manic pixie dream girl trope. She abandons her life and responsibilities to follow a man who represents freedom and nonconformity.

jokes.text: Slater to Britta: 'I thought you were all into female empowerment. What's more empowering than a woman in a crown?'
jokes.setup: Britta is ambivalent about being nominated for transfer queen
jokes.punchline: Slater weaponizes feminist language to pressure Britta into competing — a sarcastic judo move that exposes the absurdity of the crown while also being a genuine needle
jokes.explanation: Smart joke — Slater is both right and completely trolling Britta. The line twists feminist rhetoric into an argument for a beauty pageant, which is funny precisely because it's logically coherent but obviously wrong. Good character work for Slater as a measured, tactical rival.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, you mean Blade Thrustchord? I thought his name was Blade Thrust-cord.

jokes.text: Troy stumbles in having just done his first keg stand: 'Just did my first keg stand! Can't feel my legs.'
jokes.setup: Serious romantic tension scene between Jeff, Britta, and Slater
jokes.punchline: Troy bursts in with gleeful intoxication, completely puncturing the drama — 'can't feel my legs' is delivered with pure joy
jokes.explanation: Good tension-break joke. Troy's comedic timing as an oblivious interloper in serious scenes is well-established. 'Can't feel my legs' is the right level of commitment. Impact is higher than craft because Troy's energy tends to elevate the material.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I spent three hours last night deciding between two types of pens. Three hours! I made a pro-con list, I researched ink viscosity, I tested them both on different paper stocks.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: In the end, I went with the one that felt better in my hand, which is what I knew after thirty seconds.

jokes.text: Pierce's original school song: 'Dancing in your underwear, taking air conditioner repair, so you can get a job. Greendale's the way it goes.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has apparently composed an original song for Greendale Community College
jokes.punchline: The 'school song' is completely devoid of school spirit — it describes Greendale as a last resort where people study HVAC in their underwear
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier original songs in Community's history — 'dancing in your underwear, taking air conditioner repair' captures the indignity of community college in two perfect images. It's also a great Greendale meta-joke about how unglamorous the school is. The Dean's straight response ('Our original school song by the venerable Pierce Hawthorne') adds another layer. High originality for the specific lyrical choices.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I wish you two all the happiness in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I hope the rest of you get herpes.

jokes.text: Dean: 'Our original school song by the venerable Pierce Hawthorne.' — said as though Pierce is a legendary composer
jokes.setup: Pierce has just played his absurd, dignity-free school song
jokes.punchline: The Dean introduces it with the gravity of a Carnegie Hall premiere — 'the venerable Pierce Hawthorne' treats Pierce as an institution
jokes.explanation: Good Dean moment — his institutional earnestness makes absurd things sound official. 'The venerable Pierce Hawthorne' is funny because Pierce is exactly not venerable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What's the Spanish word for your situation?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I don't know, I don't speak Spanish.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'He's gonna be the next Yngwe Mackadangdang junior.' / Jeff: 'It's a hacky sack guy.' / Pierce: 'Hey, you don't have to tell us who Ingmar Mackadingdong junior is.'
jokes.setup: Britta mentions Vaughn's hacky sack distinction; Pierce references the name incorrectly
jokes.punchline: Pierce mangled 'Yngwe Mackadangdang' into 'Ingmar Mackadingdong' — accidentally creating an even funnier name while pretending to know who it is
jokes.explanation: Great callback joke. 'Ingmar Mackadingdong' is somehow funnier than 'Yngwe Mackadangdang' and Pierce's confident correction ('you don't have to tell us') while getting it wrong is classic Pierce — braggadocious incompetence. The name escalation makes this better than the original joke.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I spiked the punch.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And here come the women.

jokes.text: Annie: 'I spent three months researching backpacks before I chose the one that I use now. I don't want to be that person anymore.'
jokes.setup: Annie is explaining why she's impulsively deciding to transfer to Delaware with Vaughn — she's trying to 'live in the moment'
jokes.punchline: Her example of her old self being 'too cautious' is that she spent three months researching backpacks — the specificity of 'backpacks' as her cautionary tale is perfect Annie-calibrated anxiety
jokes.explanation: Excellent Annie joke — the backpack research is the perfect microcosm of Annie's character: obsessive, detail-oriented, risk-averse. The fact that she's using THIS as her personal growth story (not something actually consequential) is both funny and revealing. Near-perfect character integration: only Annie would choose 'backpack research' as her cautionary tale. The structure is tight — it sets up her reasoning, then the punchline deflates it completely.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You just got your ass kicked by two girls.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Well, for your and Vaughn's sake, I hope it works out. But on behalf of the rest of the group, I hope it's a catastrophe.'
jokes.setup: Jeff responds to Annie's decision to transfer to Delaware with Vaughn
jokes.punchline: He splits his response into a polite public statement and a private group wish for disaster — the 'on behalf of the rest of the group' framing is the joke
jokes.explanation: One of Jeff's best lines of the episode. The dual-track response — formal social convention versus true feeling — is structurally clean. 'On behalf of the rest of the group' elevates it from a simple mean comment to a parliamentary-sounding group endorsement of schadenfreude. Very quotable and very Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, I think what really makes us special is that we stick together as a group.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: We've got the smart one, the black one, the one with the boobs, the old one, the crazy one, and... well, there's Jeff.

jokes.text: Pierce, next to a dessert table: 'I can't believe nobody's taken this cookie.'
jokes.setup: Emotional farewell scene as the group reacts to Annie leaving
jokes.punchline: Pierce, apparently unbothered by the emotional moment, is fixated on a cookie — the visual of Pierce ignoring the drama for a dessert is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good tension-break moment. Pierce's oblivious self-absorption during an emotional beat is well-deployed here. The specific 'cookie' detail is nicely mundane.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Everyone talks about jumping the shark like it's a bad thing, but that episode of Happy Days was actually really well-written. The show had already jumped the shark before that — it jumped it in season two when Fonzie started wearing a leather jacket to a school dance.

jokes.text: Chang: 'Is there a word in Spanish for someone who used to pretend to be a professor, but was a teacher, but wasn't actually a teacher, and he's now a student?' asking Dean Pelton
jokes.setup: Chang is now a student at Greendale and encounters the Dean
jokes.punchline: Chang asks for a Spanish word for his exact humiliating situation — recognizing that his circumstances are bizarre enough to need their own vocabulary
jokes.explanation: Good self-aware Chang joke. The description is both a recap of his entire arc and a self-pity move — he's framing his humiliation as a linguistic gap rather than a personal failure. The Dean's follow-up ('you wouldn't know' since it'd be in Spanish) is a nice additional sting.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Jeff and Slater are getting back together.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What? No! That's terrible!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I was lying. I just wanted to show you how you react to everyone else's business before you even know the facts.

jokes.text: Chang: 'I will find a loophole.' / Beat / 'Then I'll kill you.'
jokes.setup: Jeff threatens Chang with expulsion for hitting a professor
jokes.punchline: Chang's first response (legal maneuvering) is immediately followed by a cheerful threat of murder — the escalation from bureaucratic to homicidal is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke. The beat between 'loophole' and 'then I'll kill you' is key — it suggests Chang considered other options and settled on murder as Plan B. The cheerful delivery of the death threat is very Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Where did you and Slater...?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: The library.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Well, it wasn't in the Conservatory with the Candlestick.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I'd go easy on that punch if I was you. I've put in a little... hot person. Hot people. There are two of them coming this way.'
jokes.setup: Pierce warns someone about the punch, implying he's spiked it with something questionable
jokes.punchline: He was just saying the punch has 'hot people' in it — meaning attractive people are approaching, not any added substance — a complete misdirection from the apparently spiked punch implication
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection joke — sets up 'he spiked the punch' and pivots completely. Pierce as matchmaker/spotter of attractive people is a fun use of his otherwise creepy tendencies. The delivery ('I've put in a little... hot person') plays well with the pause.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh come on, Britta. You're worried about couch hygiene? Have you SEEN the Dean's office bathroom? I'm pretty sure there's a civilization growing in there.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's... that's different.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Is it though? Because I'm fairly certain the couch is cleaner than Dean Pelton's entire administrative wing.

jokes.text: Pierce to Britta: 'Dudley Moore. Spray tan.' [as a physical assessment of Britta's date]
jokes.setup: Pierce is apparently appraising Britta's appearance or her date
jokes.punchline: Pierce delivers these two non-sequitur celebrity/descriptor fragments as if they constitute complete sentences — the gap between this and normal speech is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce absurdism — the non-sequitur as observation — but it doesn't quite land as sharply as other Pierce moments. The reference is dated and the structure is loose.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What?! Oh my God, are you serious?!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That is so messed up! What the actual... fried chicken?!

jokes.text: Two attractive women both say 'Hi, Jeff' simultaneously; everyone reacts with impressed surprise
jokes.setup: Pierce has flagged that two attractive women are approaching
jokes.punchline: Both say 'Hi, Jeff' at the exact same time — confirming Jeff's reputation with women in a single visual/audio beat
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff-as-charming character moment. The simultaneous greeting is a good execution of a familiar joke type. Functions more as characterization than a crafted joke.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Hello Michelle.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: You know, your name reminds me of a cat. Michelle... like 'meow-chelle.' Purr-fect name.

jokes.text: Britta and Slater both simultaneously reach to remove something from Jeff's face and compete over it
jokes.setup: Jeff's two love interests are both present; one or both notice something on his face
jokes.punchline: Both women reach for it simultaneously, the competitive subtext becoming literally physical — an unexpected escalation of the romantic tension
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy that serves the narrative — the romantic rivalry manifests as a slapstick scuffle over a bit of fluff on Jeff's face. The escalation from subtext to physical action is well-structured. 'Cleanest face ever' as Jeff's response after is the button.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Who has my car keys?

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: They're in the potato salad.

jokes.text: Jeff's response to both women fighting over his face: 'Cleanest face ever.'
jokes.setup: Britta and Slater have just physically competed to remove something from Jeff's face
jokes.punchline: Jeff acknowledges that his face is now extremely clean — deadpan understatement that treats the romantic rivalry as a grooming service
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfect economy. 'Cleanest face ever' works because it acknowledges the absurdity while pretending not to — Jeff treats the competitive attention as a mundane service outcome. Pure Jeff Winger: deflect with ego. High economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Jeff and Britta had sex.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: They did the Star-Spangled Banner.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: And before you ask, yes, it's American.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'You, me, and Jeff and rain man and big boobs and medium boobs and black boobs... We're a family.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is making a heartfelt speech to Troy about the importance of their study group
jokes.punchline: His list of 'family members' consists of Abed ('rain man') and three women described purely by their breast size — delivered as a sincere statement of love
jokes.explanation: Excellent Pierce character joke. His idea of a loving speech to Troy is filtered entirely through his oblivious, objectifying worldview — but crucially, he means every word sincerely. 'Rain man' for Abed is perfectly Pierce. 'Black boobs' (Shirley) is both racist and his version of an identifying description, all delivered as warmth. Very high character integration: only Pierce could ruin a sweet moment this specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You think you're competition? You're just a brief distraction from the real prize.

jokes.text: Annie, overhearing: 'Am I black boobs?'
jokes.setup: Pierce has listed the group members by his descriptions, including 'black boobs'
jokes.punchline: Annie's reaction is not outrage but genuine uncertainty about which body-based nickname Pierce assigned her — she wants to know where she falls in his taxonomy
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on Pierce's speech. Annie's reaction is funny because she doesn't challenge the taxonomy — she just wants to know her placement in it. The word 'black boobs' said by Annie Edison is inherently funny given her character. High economy (four words, full laugh).

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm not like Slater. I don't choose to be sexy and carefree.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm lazy.

jokes.text: Abed: 'Well, how's this for a finale vibe?' — introducing Pierce's offer to Troy to move into his mansion
jokes.setup: Jeff has been giving the moment 'finale vibe' by playing piano; Abed takes over the scene-setting
jokes.punchline: Abed frames the narrative event as a plot beat in a TV finale — meta-commentary on the episode's own structure
jokes.explanation: Classic Community Abed meta-move. He's the character who lives inside the show and outside it simultaneously. Flagging plot developments as 'finale vibe' is exactly his function and it's well-deployed here.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It was so good, we should retire the furniture.

jokes.text: Jeff's argument against him and Troy rooming together: 'Troy, you should live with someone who you like, but whose friendship wouldn't be altered because of constant irritation... that's Pierce.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is convincing Troy not to move in with him by arguing Troy should live with Pierce instead
jokes.punchline: Jeff's argument for Pierce as a roommate is that Pierce is someone whose friendship 'wouldn't be altered by constant irritation' — meaning Pierce is so irritating that the friendship has nowhere to go but up
jokes.explanation: Smart character logic — Jeff is essentially saying Pierce is irritation-proof because he's already maximally irritating. The reasoning is both mean and oddly sound, which is classic Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I won! I can't believe I actually won!

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Britta, we haven't even announced the results yet.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'If you and I move in, we jump the shark. That'll end it.' / Troy: 'Well, maybe you're ending it.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining why he and Troy shouldn't be roommates using TV terminology
jokes.punchline: Troy turns the TV metaphor back on Jeff — accusing him of 'ending it' (the friendship) by refusing to take the risk
jokes.explanation: Good meta-dialogue about their friendship using TV language. Troy's riposte is sharp — he's not usually the one who wins a verbal exchange, so this landing well for him is a minor character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I have something to say! This award ceremony represents everything wrong with hierarchical systems of validation and competitive achievement metrics. We should all reject these arbitrary distinctions and instead celebrate our collective mediocrity as equals!

jokes.text: Jeff: 'And for the record, there was an episode of Happy Days where a guy literally jumped over a shark, and it was the best one.'
jokes.setup: Jeff used the phrase 'jump the shark' in conversation; Troy called him out
jokes.punchline: Jeff defends 'jumping the shark' by claiming the original shark-jumping episode was the BEST Happy Days episode — a contrarian reframing of one of TV's most famous decline-markers
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best meta-jokes. Jeff's contrarian defense of 'jumping the shark' is both a pop-culture deconstruction and a perfect character beat — he can't let any expression stand without subverting it. The joke is also genuinely clever: technically, the Happy Days shark episode WAS a beloved piece of television history (even if it signaled decline). High originality because it's a genuinely unexpected angle on an extremely familiar reference. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: So... that was awkward. Anyway, you should really exfoliate more. Your skin could use it.

jokes.text: Shirley, referring to Slater and Jeff potentially rekindling: 'Isn't it nice that Jeff and Slater are getting back together?' — to Britta
jokes.setup: Shirley is probing Britta's feelings about Jeff
jokes.punchline: Shirley states the worst-case scenario for Britta as a cheerful positive — a subtle manipulation disguised as pleasant conversation
jokes.explanation: Good Shirley character moment — she deploys passive-aggressive sweetness as a weapon. The 'isn't it nice' construction is perfectly her. The joke is in knowing what Shirley is actually doing versus what she says.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I ate the entire cookie... the whole thing. I couldn't stop myself.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: My stomach... it feels like there's a tiny giant inside me.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait... maybe... maybe I shouldn't have eaten all of it at once?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Is the lesson here... moderation?

jokes.text: Shirley: 'Aha! And psych!' — after Britta reveals feelings about Jeff by reacting to the fake news
jokes.setup: Shirley said Jeff and Slater are getting back together; Britta reacted
jokes.punchline: Shirley immediately reveals it was a trap — 'aha! and psych!' — she made it up to get a reaction from Britta
jokes.explanation: 'Aha! And psych!' is the perfect Shirley formulation — it has an almost childlike gloating energy that's funny coming from a grown woman. The two-step reveal ('aha' then reinforcing with 'and psych') is better than just 'psych' would be.

dialogue.speaker: Slater
dialogue.line: Wait, you love me too? What a coincidence. I also love you.

dialogue.speaker: Slater
dialogue.line: You know what else is a coincidence? We're both in the same room at the same time.

jokes.text: Shirley: 'Holy macaroni with pepper Jack.' — her reaction to learning Jeff and Slater slept together
jokes.setup: Britta reveals Jeff and Slater slept together during paintball
jokes.punchline: Shirley's explosive reaction is expressed through a food-based exclamation — it has her cadence of trying to avoid actual profanity while conveying shock
jokes.explanation: 'Holy macaroni with pepper Jack' is a great Shirley line — her specific style of food-based faux-profanity is well-established, but 'with pepper Jack' adds a detail that takes it from a standard exclamation into something specifically Shirley. Near-perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Random student 1
dialogue.line: Jump!

dialogue.speaker: Random student 2
dialogue.line: Don't jump!

dialogue.speaker: Random student 3
dialogue.line: Roll to the left!

dialogue.speaker: Random student 4
dialogue.line: Yippee-ki-yay, Mr. Falcon!

jokes.text: Shirley: 'During paintball in the study room with colonel mustard.' — when asked when/where Jeff and Slater slept together
jokes.setup: Britta asks 'does it matter?'; someone (Britta) asks where
jokes.punchline: Shirley responds with a Clue reference — 'in the study room with colonel mustard' — framing the hook-up as a murder mystery
jokes.explanation: Smart pop-culture reference that actually earns its place. 'The study room with colonel mustard' captures both the location and uses the board game format to inject dark humor (treating a hookup like a Clue accusation). Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Yo, yo, yo. I'm Duncan, and I'm here to say / I rap about my rhymes in a major way / I'm British, innit, with my cup of tea / Crumpets and biscuits, that's the life for me / Big Ben, London, the Queen on the throne / Fish and chips, yeah, that's my home / I'm spittin' fire, but make it proper and tight / I'm Duncan the rapper, and I'm all right / Uh, yeah, check it.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Well, now it does matter. Where... where in the study room?' / Shirley: 'On the couches.' / Britta: 'We use those!' / Shirley: 'Oh, get over it. I've seen you shake the Dean's hand. Who knows where he's been?'
jokes.setup: Britta finds out Jeff and Slater hooked up on the study room couches
jokes.punchline: Shirley escalates from 'get over it' to implying the Dean's hands are more contaminated than any couch — the Dean's hygiene as an argument against couch anxiety
jokes.explanation: Good multi-beat escalation. The reveal of 'on the couches' triggers Britta's indignant 'we use those!', which is itself funny (she's mad about the furniture, not the relationship). Shirley's pivot to the Dean's hands is the unexpected punchline — it's both grosser than the couch situation and genuinely funny as a way to put things in perspective.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You have problems, Duncan.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Me? At least I don't have a thing for eating insects while wearing a diaper made of hundred dollar bills.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: How did you—

jokes.text: Shirley: 'Where... where in the study room?' / Annie: 'On the couches.' / Shirley: 'We use those!' / Annie: 'Oh, get over it. I've seen you shake the Dean's hand. Who knows where he's been?'
jokes.setup: Shirley is horrified by the specific location of Jeff and Britta's encounter
jokes.punchline: Annie's escalating counterargument — 'Who knows where the Dean's hand has been?' — implies the Dean's hygiene/behavior is so questionable that the couch situation is minor by comparison
jokes.explanation: The handshake as the vector of contamination rather than the couch is a funny inversion — Annie's argument is both technically sound and very strange. 'Who knows where he's been' about the Dean implies a rich off-screen life of questionable behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You're going to need a uniform.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: A uniform?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: All my houseguests wear uniforms. It's in the lease you didn't read.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I didn't think more than one person would answer the ad.' [revealing he placed a roommate ad, apparently soliciting Troy specifically]
jokes.setup: Shirley says 'do you believe in soul mates?' and Pierce says 'now don't be mad at me'
jokes.punchline: Pierce placed a roommate ad but only expected Troy to respond — implying he either only told Troy about it or the ad was designed for Troy specifically
jokes.explanation: Sweet and slightly funny — the 'dream coming true' beat followed by the reveal that Pierce's dream is surprisingly wholesome. The 'didn't think more than one person would answer' implies the ad was pretty targeted.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I wish I could live two lives. One with Britta, one with Annie.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what would solve all my problems? If you guys would all just get into some kind of weird group thing.

jokes.text: Annie's departure: group says goodbye awkwardly — 'See ya.' / 'Lates.' — after Britta's admission that none of them wanted her in the group
jokes.setup: Annie is saying goodbye before leaving; Britta reveals the group originally didn't want her
jokes.punchline: The tearful goodbye descends into awkward, dismissive farewells — 'Lates' — after the group's true initial feelings are exposed
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat — the revelation that nobody wanted Annie in the group undercuts the farewell scene. 'Lates' as a goodbye after that admission is perfect tonal deflation. The honesty ('none of us did') followed immediately by trying to continue the warm farewell is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You know, this has been quite a year. I've learned so much, grown as a person, and really found my place here at Greendale. Sure, I got a D in biology, but I'm choosing to see that as a B-minus in my heart.

jokes.text: Professor Duncan: 'Good evening, Michelle. Or may I say, meow-chelle?'
jokes.setup: Duncan approaches Slater at the dance
jokes.punchline: 'Meow-chelle' — a cat-based compliment pun attempting to say she looks great while also being an objectively terrible pickup line
jokes.explanation: Duncan's hapless flirting is funny precisely because it's so bad. 'Meow-chelle' is objectively a terrible line, which is the joke. The character-integration score is decent because Duncan's self-delusion is well-established.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Wait, who is this? And this person? I don't... I don't recognize any of these people.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I went to this school!

jokes.text: Duncan: 'Who has your car keys?' / Slater: 'They're in the taco meat.'
jokes.setup: Duncan is trying to execute a plan to leave with Slater; asks where her keys are
jokes.punchline: 'They're in the taco meat' — an entirely unexplained answer that creates an absurd image with no context
jokes.explanation: Five-word absurdist gem. 'They're in the taco meat' needs no explanation — it's funnier without one. The confidence with which it's delivered (not as a joke but as a straight answer to a straight question) makes it land harder. High quotability because it's a completely usable non-sequitur.

jokes.text: Duncan to Slater: 'What say you and I blow this pop stand and head off for a spot of slap n' tickle? I mean sex, in case the lingo hasn't made it to the States.'
jokes.setup: Duncan is attempting to pick up Slater at the dance
jokes.punchline: He uses a British euphemism ('slap n' tickle') then immediately translates it, treating America as a foreign country where his idioms haven't arrived yet
jokes.explanation: Good Duncan joke — the British-idiom-then-translation formula is well-suited to his character and the follow-up 'in case the lingo hasn't made it to the States' is funnier than the euphemism itself. High character integration: Duncan's hapless British dignity is perfectly rendered here.

jokes.text: Duncan to Slater, after learning she might leave with Jeff: 'Jeff and Britta did, uh, the Yankee Doodle.' / 'Oh, don't tell me that didn't make it to the States. It clearly originated here.'
jokes.setup: Duncan drops the bomb that Jeff and Britta slept together, using another British euphemism
jokes.punchline: 'The Yankee Doodle' as a sex act — then Duncan catches himself and acknowledges it's an American thing, not British, with 'it clearly originated here'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'The Yankee Doodle' as a sex euphemism is an inspired invention — it uses an American cultural icon for maximum absurdity. The self-correction ('it clearly originated here') is the second laugh, more sophisticated than the first. It also works as a callback to Duncan's 'in case the lingo hasn't made it to the States' line, making the structure circular. Very quotable. Earns 8+: the invention of 'the Yankee Doodle' as a sexual euphemism is genuinely original writing.

jokes.text: Britta to Slater: 'Yo, Goldilocks. Drop the smirk... You were the pit stop. He used you to numb the pain of not getting with me.'
jokes.setup: Britta is confronting Slater about Jeff
jokes.punchline: Britta's self-aggrandizing analysis — she's the destination, Slater is a pit stop — is simultaneously funny for its ego and for being delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Britta at her most confidently wrong — she frames herself as the superior option with the vocabulary of a racing metaphor. 'You were the pit stop' is a memorable line. It's also funny because we (and Slater) know Britta doesn't have this high ground.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Jeff needs a girl who doesn't just not wear underwear because Oprah told her it would spice things up. He needs a girl who doesn't wear underwear because she hasn't done laundry in three weeks.'
jokes.setup: Britta is laying out why she's better suited for Jeff than Slater
jokes.punchline: The contrast between Slater's 'aspirational no-underwear' (Oprah-endorsed) and Britta's 'depressive no-underwear' (laundry neglect) — Britta presents authentic dysfunction as a virtue
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The parallel construction — both women not wearing underwear but for completely different reasons — is an inspired structural choice. 'Oprah told her it would spice things up' vs. 'hasn't done laundry in three weeks' captures the entire Jeff/Britta vs. Jeff/Slater thematic conflict: aspiration versus authenticity. It's also an exact encapsulation of Britta as a character (she can't do grown-up maintenance but she'll make it a philosophy). Perfectly earned, completely original, and supremely quotable. This is the episode's comedic peak — approaches the 9.5 anchor in character integration and originality, falls slightly short on structure economy.

jokes.text: Britta: 'He's been to flavor country now. They should retire the table we did it on.'
jokes.setup: Britta is revealing she and Jeff have already slept together (news to Slater)
jokes.punchline: 'He's been to flavor country' as a sex metaphor (lifted from a Marlboro ad) — then 'they should retire the table' — treating their hookup as a Hall-of-Fame-caliber achievement
jokes.explanation: 'Flavor country' is a brilliant euphemism — a Marlboro Country parody applied to sex. 'Retire the table' escalates it to sports-championship territory. This is good Britta — she can't resist making herself mythological. High quotability.

jokes.text: Britta is mid-rant about Jeff and then hears her name called as nominee — 'Oh. I'm sorry, I have to go. I just won a contest for being hot.'
jokes.setup: Britta is in a charged confrontation with Slater about Jeff
jokes.punchline: She interrupts herself to attend the beauty pageant she spent the whole episode disdaining — and describes it as 'a contest for being hot' with zero irony
jokes.explanation: Excellent Britta character joke — she exits a feminist confrontation to attend the beauty contest she was supposedly above, and frames it as a 'contest for being hot' with complete self-satisfaction. The sudden pivot and the casual description of the contest she spent the episode mocking is a great character-contradiction joke. Very quotable.

jokes.text: MC listing nominees: 'This is a huge honor... I've never actually won anything before.' / MC: 'Okay, well, you still haven't. I'm just listing the nominees, so not a great time to get cocky.'
jokes.setup: Britta begins accepting the crown before she's actually won
jokes.punchline: The MC corrects her mid-speech — she hasn't won, he's just reading names — delivered with flat, bureaucratic dryness
jokes.explanation: Structurally very clean — Britta's premature victory speech is punctured by the MC's deadpan correction. 'Not a great time to get cocky' is a perfect line: understated, official-sounding, withering. Earns high scores for structure and character integration (Britta would absolutely do this) and the MC's flat delivery of an existentially crushing correction.

jokes.text: Annie, mid-nominees list, suddenly shouts across the room: 'Jeff Einger, do not get back with Slater. I love you.'
jokes.setup: The nominees are being read at the dance; Jeff is in a crisis about who to choose
jokes.punchline: Annie interrupts the ceremony completely to deliver a love confession — played both as genuine and absurd, with 'Jeff Einger' (wrong name spelling likely intentional/gag) adding a beat of comedy
jokes.explanation: Funny as a plot escalation and as an Annie character moment. The timing — interrupting an awards ceremony — is both sitcom-perfect and character-specific. 'Jeff Einger' may be a gag name or a typo, but calling him out by full name in a formal announcement style adds to the absurdity.

jokes.text: Britta leans in mid-ceremony and whispers: 'Your lipstick looks better.'
jokes.setup: Britta and Annie are both at the ceremony; Annie has just made a dramatic public declaration
jokes.punchline: Britta responds to Annie's love declaration by... complimenting her lipstick — ignoring the emotional earthquake entirely
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical callback. After Jeff called out her lipstick earlier in the episode, Britta noting Annie's improved lipstick in this heightened moment is both a callback and a great comedy-of-deflection beat. It also reveals Britta's awareness of Annie's feelings while choosing not to engage with them. Very quotable. Earns 8+ for the callback structure, economy, and tonal subversion.

jokes.text: Pierce to Troy, referring to a large cookie: 'Have you considered the 60-inch-diameter cookie you're eating?'
jokes.setup: Troy says he's sick and doesn't know why
jokes.punchline: Pierce points out Troy is eating a comically large cookie — the specific '60-inch-diameter' measurement makes it funnier than just 'big cookie'
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag — the specificity of '60-inch-diameter' elevates it. This is a physical comedy beat that relies on the absurdly large prop cookie. Good for rewatchers who can see the actual cookie.

jokes.text: Troy: 'How can something that's delicious make me sick? Unless... too much of a good thing is actually a bad thing. My friendship with Abed is a giant cookie.'
jokes.setup: Troy is sick from eating a giant cookie and trying to understand why
jokes.punchline: He extends the cookie metaphor to solve his roommate dilemma — genuinely arriving at an insight through cookie logic
jokes.explanation: One of Troy's best moments — he solves an emotional problem through literally applied food metaphor. The earnestness with which he extends cookie logic to friendship is classic Troy. 'My friendship with Abed is a giant cookie' is a genuinely memorable line. Good structure: the logical chain (delicious → sick → too much good = bad → Abed) is tight even though the conclusion is absurd.

jokes.text: Jeff's speech about Slater vs. Britta: 'Slater makes me feel like I do when I write my new year's resolutions... Britta makes me feel like the guy I am three weeks after, when I'm back to hitting my snooze button and screening my mom's phone calls.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining the emotional difference between his two love interests to Annie
jokes.punchline: The contrast — Slater as aspirational New Year's self versus Britta as the actual snooze-button-hitting, mom-call-screening true self — is both emotionally true and comedically perfect
jokes.explanation: One of the best-written jokes/speeches of the episode — competing with Joke 68 for the top spot. The New Year's resolutions metaphor is brilliantly specific: the moment of writing resolutions is a recognized collective fantasy of self-improvement, and 'three weeks after' captures the universal collapse of that fantasy. 'Screening my mom's phone calls' as the detail that marks his real self is pitch-perfect. This is the thematic heart of the episode delivered as a character joke. Earns 8.5+ on structure and character integration because it's both genuinely funny and emotionally precise. The structure — parallelism with specific contrasting details — is masterful.

jokes.text: Slater's public declaration: 'Jeff, I love you.' / Annie: 'I wonder where she got that from.' / Slater: 'I'm sorry, do you have a patent on loving people?'
jokes.setup: Slater, having heard Annie's declaration, makes her own
jokes.punchline: Annie's dry 'I wonder where she got that from' and Slater's 'patent on loving people' response escalate the situation into a comedic public spat while everything is already on fire
jokes.explanation: 'Do you have a patent on loving people?' is a good comeback — the absurdity of intellectual property law applied to declarations of love. Annie's dry side-comment is a good character beat.

jokes.text: Annie to Jeff: 'And then we could all get together for some weird foursome.'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie are discussing a fantasy of living two parallel lives — him with Slater and with Britta simultaneously
jokes.punchline: Annie extends the metaphor logically to its conclusion — if both versions of Jeff exist, all four can meet up — and uses 'weird foursome' with apparent obliviousness to its sexual implication
jokes.explanation: Good Annie joke — she says 'weird foursome' meaning a quadruple date but the word 'foursome' has obvious other implications, especially coming from Annie. The fact that she says 'weird' suggests she might half-know. Good character-specific delivery of an inadvertently loaded line.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Choose Britta.' / Troy: 'Yeah, Team Britta.' / Another voice: 'Britta's lame. Team Slater.' / Someone else: 'Bring Conan back!'
jokes.setup: Everyone is waiting for Jeff to choose between Annie and Slater (and implicitly Britta)
jokes.punchline: 'Bring Conan back!' — a completely non-sequitur audience demand that emerged from the team-choosing energy, implying someone in the crowd has been waiting for any opportunity to voice this complaint
jokes.explanation: 'Bring Conan back!' is an inspired absurdist detail — it rewards the escalation of the crowd-chanting scene by introducing a completely irrelevant demand that someone has apparently been holding onto. It's topical (referencing the Conan/Leno controversy of 2009-2010) but functions as pure absurdism. Great economy.

jokes.text: Professor Duncan takes the microphone: 'My name is Professor Ian Duncan, and I would like to rap for you. Drop a beat.' — then proceeds to badly rap: 'My name is Ian Duncan and I'm here to say / I'm going to rap to the beat in a rapping way / I've got a real big penis and I drink lots of tea'
jokes.setup: Jeff is frozen in his love-triangle crisis; Duncan decides to intervene by rapping
jokes.punchline: Duncan's rap is catastrophically bad — the lyrics are circular non-content, then he reveals his penis size and tea drinking as his two main attributes
jokes.explanation: One of Duncan's defining moments. The rap is funny on multiple levels: the self-referential filler lyrics ('I'm going to rap to the beat in a rapping way'), the British vs. American cultural cringe, and 'I've got a real big penis and I drink lots of tea' as his self-description. The escalation from meaningless boasting to absurd self-disclosure is well-paced. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'That's enough.' / Duncan: 'Why?' / Jeff: 'You have a problem.' / Duncan: 'Oh, I have a problem? Who is it here who has a dalmatian fetish?'
jokes.setup: Jeff tries to shut Duncan down; Duncan fights back
jokes.punchline: Duncan reveals Jeff has a dalmatian fetish as his rebuttal — an entirely unexpected, specific, and odd accusation deployed as a defensive weapon
jokes.explanation: Excellent surprise joke. 'Dalmatian fetish' is a perfect absurdist accusation — specific enough to be disturbing, animal enough to be unusual, breed-specific enough to be extra strange. The escalation from 'you have a problem' to 'you have a fetish for one specific dog breed' is a great comedic mismatch. Earns 8+ for originality and the absurd specificity of 'dalmatian' (not just 'dogs').

jokes.text: Jeff: 'That is an oversimplification, and you are suspended.' / Duncan: 'Oh, come on.' / Jeff: 'Oh, not a teacher anymore.'
jokes.setup: Jeff threatens Duncan with suspension for the dalmatian accusation
jokes.punchline: Jeff catches himself — he's not actually in authority here — and admits it immediately with 'Oh, not a teacher anymore'
jokes.explanation: Good self-aware beat — Jeff reflexively defaults to authority he doesn't have. The immediate self-correction is funnier than if someone else had corrected him.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'That is a oversimplification, and you are suspended.' / Duncan: 'Oh, come on.' / Jeff: 'Oh, not a teacher anymore.'
jokes.setup: Jeff responds to the dalmatian accusation
jokes.punchline: Jeff neither denies the dalmatian fetish NOR addresses the content — he only challenges the word 'oversimplification,' then pivots to suspending Duncan, only to be reminded he has no such authority
jokes.explanation: Perfect multi-beat joke. Jeff's 'oversimplification' as his only defense of the dalmatian fetish allegation is hilarious — it confirms the fetish while contesting the framing. Then his instinct to suspend Duncan, and 'Oh, not a teacher anymore' as the reminder of his powerlessness, is a great secondary beat. Strong structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Duncan produces a roll of quarters and attacks Jeff with them; they wrestle as Duncan yells 'Oh, man!' and 'He's on me! He's on me!'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Duncan have been verbally sparring
jokes.punchline: Duncan attacks Jeff with a roll of quarters — the escalation from verbal argument to physical combat with coins is absurd. 'He's on me! He's on me!' from Duncan (the instigator) is the button
jokes.explanation: Good physical escalation. Duncan's 'He's on me! He's on me!' despite being the aggressor is a funny inversion. The roll of quarters as a weapon is specific and odd in the right way.

jokes.text: Pierce to Troy, mid-fight: 'I'll do it. I'll move in with you.' / Troy: 'Fantastic, buddy!' / Pierce: 'Why don't you come over Saturday? My tailor will fit you for a uniform.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has been trying to convince Troy to live with him
jokes.punchline: Pierce's offer includes having Troy fitted for a 'uniform' by his tailor — this escalates from 'roommate' to 'servant' in one beat
jokes.explanation: Perfect Pierce joke — his wealth and obliviousness combine to offer Troy a deal that is simultaneously generous (tailor!) and insulting (servant's uniform). Troy's 'Fantastic, buddy!' before he processes the uniform detail is a great beat. High character integration.

jokes.text: Annie explains why she came back: 'I finally started living in the moment, and I realized that, in the moment, Greendale is where I belong.'
jokes.setup: Annie, who left to 'live in the moment', has come back; Jeff asks what happened
jokes.punchline: The whole point of 'living in the moment' was supposed to be spontaneous adventure — and when she did it, the conclusion was 'stay at community college'
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff for Annie's character arc in this episode. Her 'living in the moment' experiment concludes with the most unadventurous possible result — staying exactly where she started. It's sweet but also funny precisely because the moment she trusted her instincts, they kept her in community college.

jokes.text: Video yearbook confessionals — Garrett: 'Oh my God. I'm finally popular enough to be in the yearbook. What do you mean, video yearbook? Where do I sign?'
jokes.setup: End-of-year video yearbook segment; various characters give confessionals
jokes.punchline: Garrett's excitement at being included in the yearbook — then immediate re-excitement when told it's a video — reveals the depth of his social desperation
jokes.explanation: Good Garrett background-character moment. His breathless delight followed by the 'video yearbook' recalibration is a nice two-beat structure. The joke works because of Garrett's specific energy.

jokes.text: Video yearbook confessional — unnamed student: 'Photo not available.'
jokes.setup: Various students give yearbook testimonials
jokes.punchline: One student appears on camera but their identifier reads 'Photo not available' — they exist but are unrecognized even by the system documenting them
jokes.explanation: Very economical visual joke — the inherent absurdity of a video format having a 'photo not available' placeholder is good meta-comedy. It also makes a quick point about how invisible background characters are within the show's own world. Rewatch bonus because it's easy to miss.

jokes.text: Video yearbook confessional — student: 'This better not be one of those take-your-top-off videos.'
jokes.setup: Students are giving video yearbook testimonials
jokes.punchline: One student's response to being filmed is a suspicious warning about nudity — suggesting this has happened to them before at Greendale
jokes.explanation: Good Greendale-as-sketchy-institution joke. The student's paranoia implies a history of inappropriate filming. Quick and economical background gag.

jokes.text: Abed's video yearbook confessional: 'I don't believe in yearbooks.'
jokes.setup: Students are giving yearbook testimonials
jokes.punchline: Abed simply states he doesn't believe in yearbooks — delivered flatly, as if it's a philosophical position
jokes.explanation: Perfect Abed economy. 'I don't believe in yearbooks' is a funny declaration that could mean many things — he doesn't believe they exist, he doesn't believe in what they represent, he has a philosophical objection. His appearing in one while saying this is the implicit gag.

jokes.text: Pierce's video yearbook confessional: 'I just want people to remember there's a guy in between these things.' (referencing being between two attractive female classmates)
jokes.setup: Pierce is giving his yearbook testimonial
jokes.punchline: Pierce's entire motivation for being in the yearbook is to establish his presence between two attractive women — the visual of him flanked by them while saying 'there's a guy in between these things' is the full joke
jokes.explanation: Good Pierce character joke. His vanity and lechery combine in a yearbook caption that is both sad and self-aggrandizing. The visual of him clearly positioned between women makes it funnier as a physical gag.

jokes.text: Shirley's video yearbook confessional: 'What a year. Only two pregnancy scares.'
jokes.setup: Shirley is giving her year-in-review testimonial
jokes.punchline: 'Only two pregnancy scares' — framing it as a positive ('only two!') implies this is a good year by Shirley's standards
jokes.explanation: Excellent Shirley line — maximally economical and character-perfect. 'Only two pregnancy scares' implies a base rate that is both alarming and funny. The 'only' is doing all the work: it frames a troubling situation as an improvement. This is the best of the yearbook confessionals. High originality because it's both a character reveal and a dark life-commentary in four words.

jokes.text: Troy's video yearbook confessional: 'I can't believe I spent ten bucks on this.'
jokes.setup: Troy gives his year in review for the video yearbook
jokes.punchline: He's apparently watching the video he just appeared in and immediately complains about paying for it — his entire reflection on the year is buyer's remorse
jokes.explanation: Very economical Troy joke. His entire emotional takeaway from the year is 'this cost ten dollars and I regret it' — a funny anti-climax to end the yearbook segment. The specificity of '$10' is the right level of petty.

jokes.text: Final student's video yearbook confessional: 'I don't know any of these people.'
jokes.setup: The video yearbook ends with a final testimonial
jokes.punchline: The last person in the video has no connection to any of the people in the yearbook they're ostensibly commemorating — they're just a stranger who was filmed
jokes.explanation: Perfect button for the episode — completely deflationary. After all the emotional season-finale closure, the last word goes to someone who has zero relationship with any of these people. It's an anti-climax that also works as a Greendale meta-joke: the community college's community is so loose that strangers wander into the yearbook.

tmdb_overview: As the end of the school year finds Jeff at the apex of a romantic triangle, Annie ponders moving away with her hacky sack-playing boyfriend.
insight: Season finale escalates character comedy through 62 jokes in 44 minutes without hitting elite threshold.
